source.title: Training Language Models on the Knowledge Graph: Insights on Hallucinations and Their Detectability
source.authors: Jiri Hron; Laura Culp; G. Elsayed; Rosanne Liu; Ben Adlam; Maxwell L. Bileschi; Bernd Bohnet; JD Co-Reyes; Noah Fiedel; C. D. Freeman; Izzeddin Gur; Kathleen Kenealy; Jaehoon Lee; Peter J. Liu; Gaurav Mishra; Igor Mordatch; Azade Nova; Roman Novak; Aaron T. Parisi; Jeffrey Pennington; Alex Rizkowsky; Isabelle Simpson; Hanie Sedghi; Jascha Narain Sohl-Dickstein; Kevin Swersky; S. Vikram; T. Warkentin; Lechao Xiao; Kelvin Xu; Jasper Snoek; S. Kornblith

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own cross-entropy results on a KG training regime and explicitly describes the dataset-size trend as differing from established scaling results; it does not fit the original held-out-loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training loss over all tokens in formatted KG triplets, not held-out loss. Hallucination-rate and detector results are not rows because they do not measure the loss or allocation named by the claim. Scaling-law results cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study never measures held-out pretraining loss and fits no power law. Its loss results (Fig. 3) are training loss over full triplets in a multi-epoch memorisation regime. Its main results are hallucination rates and detector AUC-PR. The 'counter to standard scaling laws' dataset-size result compares training loss at fixed steps with laws stated for held-out loss. That is a related but different construct, so it cannot show whether any version holds. The Chinchilla comparison concerns model size needed for ≤5% training-set hallucination, not loss-minimising allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that for a fixed dataset, larger and longer-trained LMs hallucinate less and reach lower training loss. Larger datasets raise hallucination and training loss at fixed model size and epochs, which they attribute to non-repeated facts. They hypothesise that repeated facts in standard text make the dataset-size effect positive. Reaching ≤5% training-set hallucination needs much larger-than-Chinchilla-optimal models and 20+ epochs, at a cost to generalisation. Hallucinations of larger LMs are harder to detect.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models from scratch on structured KG triplets and reports training loss trends; it does not reproduce the original held-out-loss power-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The loss trend depends on dataset size in this KG setup: the text reports that increasing dataset size raises training loss at fixed model size and training length.

fits_no_version.finding: For a fixed KG dataset, training loss and training-set hallucination rate fall with model size (3.15M–1.61B) and training FLOPs/epochs. At fixed model size and steps, they rise with dataset size (1% vs 10%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In non-repeated factual (KG) data, training loss and recall hallucination improve with model size and epochs but worsen with dataset size at fixed model size and training length.

fits_no_version.finding: Reaching ≤5% hallucination on training data needs models about an order of magnitude larger than Chinchilla-optimal for the token count, trained 20+ epochs. Longer training raises hallucination on unseen data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorising all facts of a dataset requires compute well beyond loss-compute-optimal allocation.

record.problems: The reported loss is training loss rather than held-out loss; results are given as plots and qualitative descriptions without numerical loss values or fitted power-law exponents. The authors note that their KG data differ from typical language-model training data.

untested.parts: No held-out loss and no power-law fit in N, D or C.
No compute-optimal loss sweep. The Chinchilla comparison concerns a hallucination target.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
The KG and multi-epoch regime is studied only through training loss and hallucination rate, with no power-law form tested.
Hallucination rate falls with model size and FLOPs but is not fitted or related to pretraining loss.
No fitting choices or exponents compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'challenges' label is dropped. The rows report training loss, not held-out loss, so the dataset-size trend is not comparable to Kaplan/Hoffmann laws. The study reports no held-out (IVS) loss. All loss results are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports training loss, not held-out pretraining loss, and does not fit power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power laws fitted on small runs are used to predict the losses of larger runs.

The study does not find a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation for fixed compute. Comparing model size needed for a hallucination threshold with a cited Chinchilla estimate is not a compute-optimal loss sweep.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests a KG-based training setting and varying dataset sizes/training lengths, but does not fit or establish a power-law form. Does not test image or video models, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance is related to scale or pretraining loss.
Although the loss trend varies with dataset size in this KG setup, the study does not fit exponents, compare fitting methods, or test whether compute-optimal allocations depend on setup.

rows.subject: decoder-only transformer LMs (aggregate across tested sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and training FLOPs while training on a fixed KG dataset; reported autoregressive cross-entropy training loss.
rows.measure: Per-token average autoregressive cross-entropy training loss over subject, predicate, and object tokens
rows.value: figure only; text states larger models attain smaller loss at a fixed dataset size
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result stated in the text; the plotted runs are not separately numerically reported. This trend alone does not establish a power law.
rows.check: The measure is training loss, not held-out loss, and there is no power-law fit. Falling training loss with model size under multi-epoch memorisation does not measure what V1/V5 name. Figure only, with no numbers.

rows.subject: decoder-only transformer LMs (aggregate across tested sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Varied training FLOPs by changing training length on a fixed KG dataset; reported autoregressive cross-entropy training loss.
rows.measure: Per-token average autoregressive cross-entropy training loss over subject, predicate, and object tokens
rows.value: figure only; text states larger training FLOPs correspond to smaller loss for a fixed dataset
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result stated in the text; no numerical loss values or fitted curve are given.
rows.check: Training loss falling with more FLOPs (epochs) on a fixed small dataset reflects memorisation, not held-out power-law scaling. Figure only, with no fitted form.

rows.subject: decoder-only transformer LMs (aggregate across tested sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-loss trends across KG dataset sizes.
rows.measure: Per-token average autoregressive cross-entropy training loss over subject, predicate, and object tokens
rows.value: figure only; text states loss increases as training set size grows
rows.note: The text contrasts this direction with established scaling results for text and attributes it to the larger dataset requiring the model to learn more facts.
rows.check: Training loss rising with dataset size at fixed model size and steps is expected for training loss in a memorisation regime. It is not held-out loss, so it cannot reverse V1/V5. The rise is real but measures a different construct.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: KG training data with increasing dataset size, at fixed model size and training length
reader_labels.reason: Training loss rises rather than following the expected improving-with-more-data trend in this setting; this challenges generalising the usual scaling behaviour to this training regime (r3). The study does not establish whether the trend is or is not a power law.
